alternatives.explanation: Definitions/mechanics: the excess could be produced by the join. Possible causes are '-R' bills being partial bills rather than duplicates, several bills per PO, duplicate SKUs on a PO or bill, bill amount not equal to lines plus freight, multiple payments per bill, or PO lines that were never billed and would offset the overbilling.
alternatives.test: Profile the '-R' bills and bills per PO. Check amount = sum(lines)+freight, duplicate SKUs, multi-payment bills, bill lines not on the PO and PO lines not billed. Re-run q130.
alternatives.result: Each '-R' bill is a second bill on a PO that already has one bill. The samples carry the identical amount 12-27 days later: 1,429 POs have exactly 2 bills, 1 of them '-R', and 365,296 POs have 1 bill (q184, q185, q186). So the -R bills are duplicate billing, a separate issue, and excluding them is correct. All 368,154 bills have amount = lines + freight. There are 0 duplicate SKUs on bills or POs, 0 bills with more than one payment, 0 billed lines off the PO and 0 unbilled lines on billed POs (q187, q188, q189). q130 reproduces exactly: 13,901 over-PO bills paid in full with $3,149,433.24 excess, 5,911 short-paid to PO, 309 unpaid (q222). The arithmetic survives.

alternatives.explanation: Confounding/hidden rule: short-paying may follow a visible rule the original did not test, such as branch (the PO branch was selected in q157 but never used), season, absolute dollar size, bill size or vendor kind. It may also run in streaks: a batch of bills handled together, or a vendor flagged after one short-pay.
alternatives.test: Full-pay rate of paid over-PO bills (2016-2025) by branch, calendar month, vendor kind, absolute excess and bill amount. Also by the previous over-PO bill's outcome, both for the same vendor and in payment-date order.
alternatives.result: No rule appears. By branch the rate is 0.683-0.723 (n 1,492-1,774 each). By month it is 0.681-0.723. By kind it is 0.696-0.705. Absolute excess under $50 is paid in full at 0.703 (n=8,428), and $1,000 or more at 0.691 (n=1,601). Bills of $25k or more are paid in full at 0.717 (n=336) (q201). After a full-paid over-PO bill from the same vendor the next is full-paid at 0.698, after a short-paid one at 0.711. In payment order the figures are 0.699 and 0.707 (q213). Overall 13,901 of 19,812 paid over-PO bills, 0.702 (q234). The outcome is statistically memoryless and does not depend on size. Interpretation: a real AP match that waves through excesses of $1,000 or more as often as excesses under $50 would be unusual. 'Inconsistently applied match' is one reading. Others are a decision driven by information not in the records, or an outcome that comes from how the data was generated. These records cannot tell those readings apart.

alternatives.explanation: Definitions (WMS evidence): the claim that WMS receipts 'contradict' billed quantities assumes receipt qty is an independent count. It may simply be recorded as the PO qty.
alternatives.test: For every stock PO line, compare the WMS receipt qty with the PO qty, counting short and over receipts. Check whether stock balances ever go negative, which would hint that extra units were sold without being receipted.
alternatives.result: Of 475,391 stock PO lines, 470,300 were received. On all 470,300 the receipt equals the PO qty: 0 short, 0 over, 0 split receipts (q194). Every receipt header has exactly the PO's line count (q195). Running balances never go materially negative: 2,842 rows fall below -1e-6, but the minimum rounds to -0.00, which is floating-point noise (q230). Billing is also one-sided: of 595,478 bill lines, 0 are below the PO in quantity or cost, and 5,520 are above in quantity and 14,816 in cost (q196). Interpretation: a receipt that never differs from the PO in 470,300 lines is behaving like 'received against PO', not an independent count. 'Received qty equals PO on all 3,631 overbilled lines' therefore adds little information. It is the only record available and supports a credit request, but it does not prove the extra units were never delivered.

alternatives.explanation: The money (freight): the $207,629.02 a year of 'freight paid on fully paid bills' may be legitimate charges, not a leak.
alternatives.test: Split full-paid freight into matched and over-PO bills, and compare the full-pay rate on freight bills with the over-PO rate.
alternatives.result: $2,076,290.17 of freight was paid in full over 10 years (q234). Of this, $1,956,020.09 sits on 14,170 bills whose lines match the PO exactly, and $120,270.08 on 875 over-PO bills (q222). Freight-bearing bills are paid in full at 0.700, against 0.702 for over-PO bills (q230, q234), so the same uniform pattern applies. There are no freight terms in the data. The freight is not shown to be excess, and adding it to make $522,572.34 a year is not supported.

alternatives.explanation: Missing data/recovery: the excess may already have been recovered through vendor credits. If so, the paid-in-full figure overstates the loss.
alternatives.test: Match vendor credits to over-quantity bill lines by vendor and SKU within 252 operating days after the bill, comparing qty and amount.
alternatives.result: There are 1,234 vendor credits totalling $1,929,606.50, each at least $393.38. They match by vendor, SKU and window to 147 over-quantity bills. Quantity matches by coincidence on 230 pairs, but the credit amount equals the billed excess on 0 (q191). WMS shows 1,465 return_vendor movements (q192). Interpretation: the credits look like returns to vendors, not overbill recoveries, so no recovery is visible. Absence of a link is not proof that nothing was recovered.

alternatives.explanation: Trend/period: the 10-year average could be driven by one period.
alternatives.test: Paid-in-full excess, stock quantity excess and freight by year.
alternatives.result: Paid-in-full excess was $423,467.54 in 2016 and $270,039.09-$332,254.38 in 2017-2025. The 2023-2025 average is $308,642.46, and the average excluding 2016 is $302,885.08 a year. Stock quantity excess ran $66,379.15-$107,268.69 a year, averaging $81,673.99 in 2023-2025 (q209, q219). The figure is a level, not a spike. The 10-year average is slightly lifted by 2016.

alternatives.explanation: The money (what is recoverable): $314,943.32 a year is 'paid above PO value'. It is not a loss.
alternatives.result: Of the $3,149,433.24, $2,317,669.52 is extra quantity valued at PO cost and $831,763.72 ($83,176.37 a year) is unit cost above PO (q222, q234). The two add up exactly, so nothing is double-counted. The unit-cost part cannot be called overbilling without contract prices. Of the quantity part, only stock lines ($839,490.41, $83,949.04 a year, q219, q234) have even a WMS record against them, and per the alternative above that record is weak. Special-order quantity has no receipt at all.

what_changed: The counts, dollars and vendor-uniformity numbers survive and reproduce exactly (q222). Three things changed. (1) The 'about 70% in every segment' result now also holds across branch, month, vendor kind, absolute dollar size, bill size and the previous bill's outcome (q201, q213). That makes it look less like a control applied inconsistently by people and more like an outcome with no recorded driver, possibly an artefact of how the data was made; 'inconsistently applied match' is downgraded to one interpretation among several. (2) 'Contradicted by WMS' is weakened. Receipts equal the PO qty on all 470,300 received stock lines and are never short (q194), so they behave like receipting against the PO, not an independent count. Billing is also never below the PO (q196). (3) The $207,629.02 a year of freight and the $522,572.34 combined figure are dropped. Most of that freight ($1,956,020.09 of $2,076,290.17) is on bills that match the PO exactly, and nothing shows freight was not owed (q222). The headline $314,943.32 a year stays, but as 'paid above PO value', not as loss. The recoverable-evidence figure is $83,949.04 a year (stock quantity), with weaker evidence than claimed. Vendor credits do not offset the excess (q191).
revised_conclusion: Excluding duplicate '-R' bills, 2016-2025: 20,121 bills exceed PO value. Of these, 13,901 were paid in full, carrying $3,149,433.24 above PO ($314,943.32 a year; 2016 high at $423,467.54, 2023-2025 average $308,642.46), 5,911 were short-paid exactly to PO value and 309 are unpaid (q222, q209, q219, q234). The over-PO rate and the roughly 70% full-pay rate are flat across all 44 vendors, branches, months, years, sizes and terms. Whether a bill is short-paid is not predicted by any recorded attribute, including size of the excess or the prior bill's outcome (q201, q213). There is no sign that particular vendors are behind it; OEM vendors carry most of the dollars because their units cost more. The excess splits into $831,763.72 of unit cost above PO, which cannot be judged without contract prices, and $2,317,669.52 of extra quantity. Of the extra quantity, $839,490.41 ($83,949.04 a year) is on stock lines where WMS records receipt of the PO quantity. That WMS record never differs from the PO on any line, so it supports a credit request but does not prove non-delivery (q194). Freight is not shown to be excess. No vendor credit matches any overbill (q191). Interpretation: the money paid above PO is real in the records, and nothing in the data explains why some over-PO bills are short-paid and others are not. Whether that reflects an AP practice or how the records were produced cannot be told from this data. Action: confirm with AP whether a bill-vs-PO match exists and how exceptions are released. Request vendors' delivery proofs for stock quantity overbills before claiming credits.
not_evidence_of: Not evidence that any vendor overbills on purpose, or that anyone approving payments did anything wrong. It does not show the paid excess is a loss: unit costs or freight may be contractually owed, extra units may have been delivered and receipted only up to the PO quantity, and recoveries may exist outside the records. It is not evidence of a vendor-specific problem. It is not evidence that the 70/30 split reflects human decisions, since its uniformity across every dimension tested fits a recording or generation artefact just as well. The '-R' duplicate bills (1,429, $4,196,810.04, q184) are outside this finding and deserve their own review.
